rv.q: The breathless, brilliant show has somehow only gotten stronger in its Broadway transfer from the Vineyard Theatre, where its 2020 run was cut short by the pandemic.
Both play and performance are a gift we are lucky to receive, as this Broadway season shapes up to be a landmark one for its presentation of unconventional new plays and revelatory performances.
What else would a playwright do to make reparations but write a play about just that, in the process returning to her what the world had stolen: her voice.
It is also a voice lost in a haze of realities, roles and identities that will have audiences transfixed throughout the show's 75 minutes.
The result is a piece of theater unlike anything else on Broadway.
O'Connell is nothing less than astonishing.
It is the least likely show ever to make its way uptown where it’s now the best play on Broadway.
After 18 months of true crime podcasts and TV shows at home, Dana H. expands the genre into the theatrical sphere and establishes itself as one of the best plays in the season.
Her mesmerizing account of a five-month waking nightmare pulls us so deeply into the psyche of abuse that we fully comprehend the utter surrender, the no-way-outness.
This is a singular, richly nuanced performance.
That makes Dana H. inspirational in the best way: If she can laugh at her captor, you can laugh at the boss or neighbor or petty tyrant on the PTA who is making your life miserable.
Nonetheless, he has written a theatre piece that unmistakably demands considerable thought and even more unmistakably boasts Deirdre O’Connell’s unbounded talents.
Still, the most astonishing part about Dana H. is its utter lack of bitterness and rage.
At its best, the production is compelling, terrifying, and multilayered.
Her performance is a rare combination of technical perfection and theatrical séance.
This act of storytelling, through the gifted intermediary of O’Connell, can, I hope, work as the same sort of release from this period in her life.
That thought, and O’Connell’s incredible work, will both linger in the mind long after “Dana H.” ends.
Some stories are just so weird that you are left with more questions at the end of the telling than at the beginning.

cn.t: Critics hail this uncanny docudrama as mesmerizing and unforgettable, with Deirdre O'Connell's stunning lip-sync performance of a harrowing abduction story blurring the line between theater and documentary in deeply unsettling ways.

sg.ra: Center orchestra rows D-G offer head-on sightlines to the high stage without neck strain. Gentle rake; intimate 922-seat house means even mid-orchestra feels close. Playbill notes Oh, Mary! action is downstage center, rewarding central seats.

Telecharge lists extreme sides of the first 11 orchestra rows as obstructed-view seats per Playbill. SeatPlan confirms double-digit seats are angled with far-side stage obstruction. 1903 house geometry leaves sharp side angles near stage.

sg.n: Orchestra Rear (Rows L-O, behind mezz overhang)
sg.ra: TickPick and SeatPlan both confirm Mezzanine overhang begins at Row L of Orchestra. AVFMS reviewer for O12 praised tiered rake ('raised above the row in front so you don't have any heads blocking you'). Fine for plays; top-of-stage cutoff limits tall-set musicals.

SeatPlan: 'patrons can look directly down to the stage, taking advantage of the Mezzanine's fantastic aerial views which don't sacrifice detail.' Excellent rake prevents blocked views. Ideal for spectacle/musicals where staging composition matters.

Folliesbroadway and Headout both flag Mezz D-F center as best value: clean sightlines, excellent rake, priced materially below front-mezz/prime-orchestra. Balcony overhang doesn't cut in until Row C so D-F also sit past the cutoff line without being affected (SeatPlan note is about row C).

sg.n: Mezzanine Rear (behind Row C — balcony overhang) and Side Double-Digits
sg.ra: SeatPlan: 'Balcony overhang kicks in at row C, so views behind this may experience cut-off at the top of the stage.' Double-digit side seats (D24, G22) have partial sightlines. Fine for plays; poor for tall scenic musicals.

Rows B and C clear the Row A safety rail and preserve a steep but clean center view. Tripadvisor: 'Great view of the stage, although a bit of an angled view down.' Starting prices on SeatPlan as low as $68-$80. Steep rake is uncomfortable but preserves sightlines.

sg.n: Balcony Row A and Side L/R front rows
sg.ra: Row A front has a safety rail that cuts across the stage (SeatPlan, Playbill, Tripadvisor all independently confirm). TickPick: Balcony L and R first two rows have partial views due to railing. Shorter patrons especially affected.
